title: The Last Dinner on the Floor

pages.text:
The power died at 4:00 sharp. The refrigerator hummed for three seconds, then stopped, and the house went dark with a silence that felt heavier than the boxes stacked in the hall. Mom stood in the kitchen, clipboard clutched to her chest, her pencil hovering uselessly over the air. She tried to read the list, but without the overhead light, the paper was just a white rectangle of panic.

The phone rang. It was the trucking company. They were coming at six a.m., not seven. The schedule had shifted. Mom’s shoulder dropped. She looked at the empty fridge, then at the wall, then at me. Her eyes did that thing where they look through you, like you are a window she was looking out of.

I took the clipboard from her hands. I didn’t ask. I just took it. I opened it to the first page, where the list started with a column of empty boxes. I uncapped my pen. I wrote two words at the very top: Dinner. I drew a big, thick checkmark next to it.

"Trust me," I said.

I put the clipboard back in her hands. She looked at the checkmark, then at my face, and for the first time all day, her shoulders unclenched. She didn't know why. But she nodded.
pages.image: Max hands a clipboard to his mother in a dimly lit kitchen; she looks stunned; a single candle flame glows on the counter; cardboard boxes stacked high in the background.

pages.text:
We dragged the table out and shoved the boxes into the corners, clearing a space that felt like a stage. I went to the garage and hauled out Dad’s old camping stove, the one with the dented lid that stuck, and lit the candles. One, two, three. The light was orange and low, turning the dust motes into tiny gold specks floating in the air.

Dad sat cross-legged on the rug, looking at the stove, then at the pot of tuna noodle casserole I had warmed up. "You know," he said, his voice thick with a pun that was about to explode, "I was going to say this was a pot luck, but then I realized it was more of a... fire drill."

Tessa was already tapping her drumsticks against the empty pot. *Tink, tink, tink.* It was a rhythm, fast and sharp. Gus sat in the dinosaur hood, staring at the candle flames. He leaned in. He leaned in more. He roared. Not a scary roar. A happy one. The flame flickered but didn't go out.

Waffles trotted in, stole a slipper, and left it in the middle of the carpet. Nobody chased him. Nobody cared. The house felt warm, and the air smelled like tuna and wax, and for a second, none of us looked at the wall where the posters used to be. We just looked at each other.
pages.image: A group sits on the living room floor around a small camping stove; candles in jars provide warm light; a boy in a green T. rex costume leans toward a flame; a corgi with a slipper in its mouth walks away.

pages.text:
"Okay," I said. "Rules. One thing. What are we taking with us? What are we missing?"

Dad went first, scratching his mustache as he thought. "The toast," he announced, leaning forward with genuine pride. "Specifically, the way it tastes like charcoal and yet I keep eating it."

Tessa shrugged, tapping a drumstick once against her knee. "The garage, and the fact that I can be loud and nobody tells me to stop."

Gus pointed his claw at the carpet. "The floor," he said simply. "It’s soft."

I waited, letting the quiet settle around us like a thick layer of peanut butter, heavy and sweet instead of empty.

"I’ll miss this floor, and Waffles under the table, and Dad’s toast, and the way every one of you is loud," I said, looking at each of them in turn. "And I’ll take it with me, because that’s the whole trick. It goes in a pocket."

Dad wiped his mouth with his fish apron and didn’t say anything, just smiling with the kind of real warmth that doesn't need a pun to back it up. Mom picked up her pencil and wrote something on her clipboard, her brow furrowing in concentration. I didn’t look at what she wrote, because I didn’t need to.
pages.image: A boy in a red hoodie sits on a rug, looking at his family; his father in a fish apron smiles; a girl with purple hair streaks taps a pot; a small child in a dinosaur costume points at the floor.

pages.text:
At 11:58, the house was quiet. The candles had shrunk to useless nubs. My family lay in a tangle of air mattresses and blankets, breathing slow. I stood in the hallway, alone with the clock. The face was dark. I didn’t look up at the door. I didn’t wait for Gerald. I just talked to the wood and the paint.

"Thanks," I said. "If you want to do a hundred and one, that’s okay. I’d rather be here happy than there happy-later. But I think it’s time."

The old feeling tugged at my stomach, the fear that letting go meant losing everything. I let it go. I didn’t wish. I didn’t ask. I just stood there and listened to the second hand tick. It didn’t matter where the tick went. It only mattered that I was listening. The day wasn’t a math problem I had to solve. It was just a thing that happened, and I had been inside it. That was enough.
pages.image: A boy stands alone in a hallway, looking at a cuckoo clock; the scene is dimly lit by moonlight from a window; the clock face is dark; the boy's expression is calm and resolved.

pages.text:
The little door opened.

Gerald popped out, looking small in the dark hallway. His painted eyes held a tired, gentle weight that reminded me of the last frame of a movie after the credits roll. He opened his beak.

"Cuck-oo."

It was quiet, almost like a sigh escaping a deflated soccer ball.

"Good night, Gerald," I said.

I turned and walked up the stairs without running or looking back. On the third step, I saw my family asleep on the air mattresses, a tangled mess of dark hair and red hoods and green spikes. I smiled, and this time it wasn't the tight, fake grin I had worn on the first Saturday, but a soft, real one that felt like a warm towel.

I lay down on my mattress and closed my eyes. The air in the room was cool and still. I fell asleep on purpose, and I did not once ask what would happen next.
pages.image: A boy lies on an air mattress in a dark room, eyes closed and smiling gently; soft candlelight glows in the background; the scene is peaceful and quiet.
